title: Recursion · data structures and classes in Python (Lecture 03, Lab 03)

questions.stem: Every correct recursive function needs:
options: a base case, and a recursive case that moves closer to the base case
a loop and a return statement
a global variable to count the calls
questions.explanation: A base case that answers directly, and progress towards it. A loop (b) is not needed; one recursive call (c) is enough; a global counter (d) is a debugging aid, not a requirement.

questions.stem: With def factorial(n): return 1 if n == 0 else n * factorial(n - 1), what does factorial(-1) do?
questions.explanation: −1, −2, −3, … moves away from the base case 0, so the calls never stop until Python's depth limit. ValueError (c) is what the exercise version should raise — by checking n < 0 explicitly.

questions.stem: By default, CPython stops a recursion at a depth of about:
questions.explanation: sys.getrecursionlimit() is 1,000 by default.

questions.stem: How much stack space does factorial(n) use?
questions.explanation: n + 1 frames are on the stack at the deepest point (n down to 0). Space is decided by the depth, not by the answer's size (d).

questions.stem: T(n) = T(n/2) + c solves to:
questions.explanation: Unroll: c is added once per halving, log2 n times.

questions.stem: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + c solves to:
questions.explanation: The number of calls doubles at every level: 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2n-1.

questions.stem: T(n) = T(n-1) + cn solves to:
questions.explanation: cn + c(n-1) + … + c = c n(n+1)/2.

questions.stem: How many moves does Towers of Hanoi need for 5 disks?
questions.explanation: 25 - 1 = 31.

questions.stem: How many subsets does a set of 4 items have (including the empty set and the whole set)?
questions.explanation: Each item is either in or out: 24 = 16. (24 (c) is 4!, the number of permutations.)

questions.stem: How many orderings (permutations) do 4 distinct items have?
questions.explanation: 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24.

questions.stem: How many calls in total does the naive fib(5) make (counting the first)?
questions.explanation: fib(5) calls fib(4) and fib(3), and so on: the recursion tree has 15 nodes. (In general 2 fib(n+1) - 1.) 8 (b) is the value fib(6).

questions.stem: Fast power written as half = power(x, n // 2) * power(x, n // 2) (then × x if n is odd). Its cost is:
options: O(n) — two calls on n/2 undo the saving
questions.explanation: Two calls on n/2: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + c = O(n). Compute the half power once, store it, and square the variable: O(log n).

questions.stem: list_max(values) recurses on values[1:]. Its running time is:
options: O(n2) — every slice copies the rest
questions.explanation: Each call copies the rest of the list: (n-1) + (n-2) + … = O(n2) — the hidden loop from Lecture 02.

questions.stem: Memoisation means:
options: storing the answer to each subproblem the first time and looking it up after
printing each call to debug it
questions.explanation: Solve each subproblem once, store its answer (for Fibonacci, in an Array indexed by n), and look it up afterwards.

questions.stem: hanoi(20) makes over a million calls. At most how many frames are on the call stack at the same time?
questions.explanation: Frames are popped as calls return; the deepest chain is hanoi(20) → hanoi(19) → … → hanoi(1): about 20 frames. The total number of calls is exponential; the depth is linear.

questions.stem:
What does f(3) print?

def f(n):
    if n == 0:
        return
    print(n, end=" ")
    f(n - 1)
    print(n, end=" ")
questions.explanation: Each call prints n on the way down, then again on the way back up, after the inner call has returned: 3 2 1 then 1 2 3.

questions.stem: What should subsets([]) return?
questions.explanation: The empty set has exactly one subset — itself. Returning [] (b) means "no subsets", and every result built from it is then empty too.

questions.stem: Tail-call optimisation in Python:
options: is done automatically for every tail call
is not done: every recursive call costs a stack frame
is done only when sys.setrecursionlimit is called
turns recursion into a loop at compile time
questions.explanation: Python deliberately keeps every frame (it keeps tracebacks complete). Deep recursion should become a loop.

questions.stem: marks = [3, 1, 2]; result = marks.sort(). What is result?
questions.explanation: sort() sorts in place and returns None. sorted(marks) returns the new list.

questions.stem: What is type({})?
questions.explanation: {} is an empty dictionary; an empty set is set().

questions.stem: The average cost of x in s for a Python set of n items is:
questions.explanation: A set is a hash table: average O(1) membership. A list would be O(n).

questions.stem:
What is wrong with this class?

class Dog:
    tricks = []
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def add_trick(self, trick):
        self.tricks.append(trick)
questions.explanation: tricks is a class variable: one list shared by every instance. Create per-object data in __init__: self.tricks = [].

questions.stem: Calling a function that contains yield:
options: runs the body and returns the first yielded value
returns a generator object without running the body yet
runs the whole body and returns a list
questions.explanation: The body only starts running when next() is called — by a for loop, list() and so on.

questions.stem: Why should a queue not be a Python list used with pop(0)?
options: lists cannot hold more than 1,000 items
pop(0) shifts every remaining item, O(n) per dequeue
pop(0) removes the last item, not the first
questions.explanation: Every remaining item shifts one place left. Use collections.deque in plain Python — or, in this course, your own CircularQueue (Week 7).

questions.stem:
What is counts after this?

counts = {}
for w in "a b a".split():
    counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
questions.explanation: get(w, 0) supplies 0 for a missing key, so no KeyError.

questions.stem: The recurrence of naive Fibonacci, T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + c, grows like:
questions.explanation: Each call spawns two subtrees almost as large as itself; the call count grows by a factor of about the golden ratio, 1.618, per step of n.

questions.stem:
Lecture 03's to_binary:

def to_binary(n):
    if n < 2:
        return str(n)
    return to_binary(n // 2) + str(n % 2)

What does to_binary(6) return?
questions.explanation: to_binary(6) = to_binary(3) + "0" = (to_binary(1) + "1") + "0" = "110". The leading digits come from the recursive call, and the last digit is added on the way back up. (a) is the digits in the order they are computed, last first, which is what you would get by putting str(n % 2) before the call; (c) adds a digit too many; (d) is the decimal number unchanged.

questions.stem: With the course gcd (return a if b == 0, else return gcd(b, a % b)), how many calls does gcd(48, 18) make in total, counting the first?
questions.explanation: gcd(48, 18) → gcd(18, 12) → gcd(12, 6) → gcd(6, 0), which returns 6: four calls. (b) forgets the last call, the one that reaches the base case b == 0; (c) confuses the number of calls with the size of b. Euclid's algorithm is O(log min(a, b)), so the count stays small.

questions.stem:
In binary_strings, the base case is changed from return [""] to return []. What does binary_strings(2) return now?

def binary_strings(n):
    if n == 0:
        return []
    shorter = binary_strings(n - 1)
    return ["0" + s for s in shorter] + ["1" + s for s in shorter]
questions.explanation: binary_strings(0) now returns [], so both comprehensions in binary_strings(1) loop over nothing and return [], and so does every call above it. There is exactly one string of length 0, the empty string, which is why the base case must be [""]. There is no infinite recursion (d): n still goes down to 0. (c) is the correct answer with the original base case.

questions.stem: flatten descends only into items for which isinstance(item, list) is true, not into everything that is iterable. Why?
options: strings are immutable, so extend cannot be called on them
isinstance is faster than checking for iterability
a one-character string contains itself, so descending into strings never reaches a base case
lists are the only iterable type in Python
questions.explanation: The string "ab" is iterable; its item "a" is also a string, and the item of "a" is "a" again, so the recursion never shrinks and ends in RecursionError. (a) is true of strings but has nothing to do with it; (b) is not the reason; (d) is false, since strings, tuples, sets, dicts and ranges are all iterable.

questions.stem: With the course's fast power (one call on exponent // 2, base case exponent == 0), at most how many frames of power are on the call stack at once during power(2, 1000)?
questions.explanation: The exponents are 1000, 500, 250, 125, 62, 31, 15, 7, 3, 1 and 0: one frame each, 11 at the deepest point, about log₂ n. (b) and (d) describe an O(n)-deep power; (c) ignores the frames that are waiting for their recursive call to return.

questions.stem: The memoised fib_memo(30) of Lecture 03 (memo in an Array) makes how many calls in total, counting the first?
questions.explanation: Each fib_memo(k) for k from 2 to 30 computes its value once, making two calls; after that it is looked up. That is 29 × 2 calls plus the first one: 59, against 2,692,537 for the naive fib(30) (c). (a) and (d) count the values computed, not the calls; a call that only looks up a stored answer still counts.

questions.stem: The course merge_sorted is called on two sorted lists of 600 numbers each, and raises RecursionError. Why?
options: its slices copy the lists, which costs O(n2) time
the two lists hold equal values, so the merge is not stable
a Python list cannot be longer than about 1,000 items
it makes one nested call per item it outputs: about 1,200 frames deep, past the limit of about 1,000
questions.explanation: Every call outputs one item and makes one nested call on the rest, so the depth is len(left) + len(right) = 1,200, past CPython's limit of about 1,000 frames. (a) is a real cost, but it makes the merge slow, not crash; (b) equal values are fine; (c) lists can hold millions of items. This is why merge sort's real merge, in Week 10, is a loop.

questions.stem: merge_sorted compares the heads with left[0] <= right[0]. What would change if it used < instead?
options: equal values would be lost from the result
on a tie the head of right would go first, so the merge would no longer be stable
it would raise an error when two heads are equal
questions.explanation: With <, a tie takes the head of right first, so two equal keys swap their original order: the merge is still correct but not stable, and the test with (1, "L") and (1, "R") catches it. No value is lost (a), because one of the two heads is always taken; the cost is unchanged (b); equal values compare without error (d).

questions.stem: sum_digits(n) makes one call on n // 10 and does O(1) work besides. Its running time, in terms of the number n, is:
options: O(log n) — one call per decimal digit
O(n) — one call per unit of n
O(1) — the work per call is constant
questions.explanation: T(d) = T(d-1) + c in the number of digits d, so O(d), and a number n has about log₁₀ n digits: O(log n). (b) would be right for a recursion on n − 1, not on n // 10; (c) forgets that there is one call per digit.

questions.stem: With Lecture 03's depth (0 for a non-list; otherwise 1 + the deepest item, where an empty list has depth 1), what is depth([1, [2, [3]], []])?
questions.explanation: depth(1) = 0, depth([2, [3]]) = 1 + depth([3]) = 1 + 1 = 2, and depth([]) = 1 + 0 = 1. The outer list is 1 + max(0, 2, 1) = 3. (a) forgets to count the outer list; (b) counts the empty list as if it were nested inside the deepest one.

questions.stem: In the recursive solution of Towers of Hanoi with n disks, how many times does the largest disk move?
questions.explanation: The largest disk moves once, in the middle: before that move all n − 1 smaller disks go to the spare peg, and after it they come back on top. (c) is how often the smallest disk moves (W3-M38); (d) would mean the largest disk is moved off its target, which the algorithm never does.

questions.stem: In the moves returned by hanoi(n), how many times does the smallest disk move?
questions.explanation: Disk k (1 is the smallest) moves 2n-k times, so the smallest disk moves 2n-1 times: on every other move, every odd-numbered one. For n = 4 the counts are 8, 4, 2, 1, which add up to 24 - 1 = 15. (c) is the total number of moves; (a) is the largest disk.

questions.stem: Why is gcd easy to rewrite as a plain while loop, while hanoi would need an explicit stack?
options: gcd makes one call as its very last action; hanoi branches, and must remember work still to do after each call
hanoi cannot be written without recursion at all
Python optimises the tail call in hanoi, but not the one in gcd
questions.explanation: In gcd, the call return gcd(b, a % b) is the last thing done, so nothing has to be remembered: overwrite a and b and go round again. hanoi makes two calls and has work left after the first (move the largest disk, then the second call), and the call stack is what remembers it; a loop version must keep that stack itself. (b) is reversed; (c) is false, since any recursion can be a loop with a stack; (d) is false, since Python does no tail-call optimisation at all.

questions.stem: Lecture 03's array_max(arr, i=0) recurses on i + 1 and never slices. What happens when it is called on a course Array of 5,000 numbers?
options: it returns the maximum in O(n) time and O(1) space
it returns the maximum, but in O(n2) time
it raises RecursionError: one frame per element, and 5,000 is past the limit of about 1,000
questions.explanation: No slicing means no copying, so the time is O(n), but each element still costs a frame: the depth is n, and 5,000 frames is past the limit. That is why (a) is wrong: the space is O(n), not O(1). (b) is the cost of the slicing version, list_max.

questions.stem:
The course subsets:

def subsets(items):
    if not items:
        return [[]]
    rest = subsets(items[1:])
    return rest + [[items[0]] + subset for subset in rest]

What does subsets([1, 2]) return, in this order?
questions.explanation: subsets([2]) is rest + [[2] + s for s in rest] with rest = [[]], so [[], [2]]. Then subsets([1, 2]) is [[], [2]] (the subsets without 1) followed by [[1], [1, 2]] (the same with 1 in front). (a) is the same subsets in another order, which the tests would also accept after sorting, but it is not what this code returns.

questions.stem: Which of these can be used as a dict key or a set member?
questions.explanation: A key must be hashable, and the hash must not change: a tuple of hashable values is immutable, so it qualifies. A list (a), a dict (b) and a set (c) are mutable, and Python raises TypeError: unhashable type. Use frozenset if you need a set as a key.

questions.stem:
What does this print?

t = (1, [2])
t[1].append(3)
print(t)
options: (1, [2, 3]) — the tuple cannot change which objects it holds, but the list inside it can change
questions.explanation: The tuple stores two references, and these cannot change: you cannot write t[1] = [9]. But the list that t[1] refers to is itself mutable, and append changes it in place, with no error (b). (c) would be true only if the list had been copied into the tuple; (d) confuses the list with its items.

questions.stem:
What does this print?

def countdown(n):
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1

g = countdown(3)
next(g)
print(list(g))
questions.explanation: Calling countdown(3) runs nothing yet. next(g) runs the body as far as the first yield and returns 3, which is thrown away. list(g) resumes from there and collects the rest: 2 and 1. (a) forgets that 3 has already been used; (b) would be the answer if next had used up the whole generator.

essays.stem: Draw the call stack at every step of factorial(3), from the first call until the final value is returned. Label winding, the base case, and unwinding, and show the value each frame returns.
essays.answer:
— writing f for factorial, the stack at each step, bottom → top (Lecture 03's figure draws the same thing for factorial(4)):

StepStackWhat happens
1f(3)calls f(2)
2f(3) f(2)calls f(1)
3f(3) f(2) f(1)calls f(0)
4f(3) f(2) f(1) f(0)base case: f(0) returns 1
5f(3) f(2) f(1)1 × 1 = 1; f(1) returns 1
6f(3) f(2)2 × 1 = 2; f(2) returns 2
7f(3)3 × 2 = 6; f(3) returns 6

Marking points: each call pushes a frame with its own n; nothing is multiplied during winding; the base case stops the growth; each return pops a frame and the frame below finishes its multiplication; maximum depth 4 = n + 1.

essays.stem: Explain why the naive recursive Fibonacci takes exponential time, using a recursion tree. Show how memoisation fixes it, and state the new time and space costs.
essays.answer:
• fib(n) calls fib(n-1) and fib(n-2); the recursion tree roughly doubles with each increase in n, because each node has two children almost as large as itself.
  • The same subproblems are recomputed many times: in fib(5), fib(2) is computed 3 times, fib(3) twice. Total calls 2 fib(n+1) - 1 — exponential, about 1.618n; fib(30) makes 2,692,537 calls.
  • Memoisation: store each fib(k) in a memo Array the first time it is computed; later calls look it up. Each value is computed once.
  • New cost: O(n) time (2n − 1 calls — 59 for n = 30), O(n) space for the memo plus O(n) stack depth.

essays.stem: When should you prefer recursion, and when a loop? Include two concerns that are specific to Python.
essays.answer:
• Recursion when the data or the problem is recursive: trees, nested lists, grammars; divide and conquer (binary search, merge sort); branching searches (subsets, Hanoi, backtracking) — where it is clearer and the depth is small.
  • A loop when the recursion would be one call per element of flat data, or the depth could be large.
  • Python concerns, any two: the ~1,000-frame recursion limit (RecursionError); no tail-call optimisation, so every call costs a frame; a function call is relatively slow in CPython; slicing inside recursion silently adds O(n) per call.

essays.stem: Describe the recursive strategy for Towers of Hanoi. Write its recurrence, solve it, and explain why no algorithm can use fewer moves.
essays.answer:
• Strategy for n disks from A to C: move n − 1 disks A → B (recursively, using C as spare); move the largest disk A → C; move the n − 1 disks B → C (recursively, using A as spare). Base case: one disk, one move.
  • Recurrence: T(1) = 1, T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1.
  • Solution: T(n) = 2n - 1 (unroll: 1, 3, 7, 15, …; or the induction proof in W3-R5).
  • Minimum: the largest disk must move at least once. At that moment all the other n − 1 disks must be on the spare peg — which takes at least T(n-1) moves — and afterwards they must all be moved back on top, at least T(n-1) more. So any solution needs at least 2T(n-1) + 1 moves: the exponential cost is in the problem, not the algorithm.

essays.stem: Explain "trust the recursion" and how it relates to mathematical induction.
essays.answer:
• When writing the recursive case, assume the recursive call correctly solves the smaller problem, and only ask how to build this answer from that one. Do not trace every call.
  • This is induction: the base case is the induction base; "if the smaller call is right then this call is right" is the inductive step. Together they prove the function correct for every input the measure reaches.
  • It only works if the base case is right and the recursive case really makes progress towards it.

essays.stem: For each job, choose list, tuple, set or dict and justify by cost: (a) the marks of a class, in the order entered; (b) checking whether a student ID has already been registered; (c) looking up a student's name by ID; (d) one student's (ID, name, mark), used as a key elsewhere.
essays.answer:
• (a) list — ordered, grows by append in amortised O(1), allows duplicates (two students can have the same mark).
  • (b) set — "have I seen this ID?" is O(1) on average against O(n) for a list; duplicates are exactly what it prevents.
  • (c) dict — ID → name, O(1) average lookup by key.
  • (d) tuple — a fixed record of related values of different types; immutable, therefore hashable, so it can be a dictionary key or set member (a list cannot).

essays.stem: hanoi(20) makes over a million calls, yet it never has more than about 20 frames on the call stack. Explain why the space a recursion needs is set by its depth and not by its number of calls. Give the depth of factorial(n), of the fast power(x, n) and of hanoi(n), and explain why raising sys.setrecursionlimit is not the right fix for a recursion that must go 100,000 deep.
essays.answer:
• A frame exists only while its call is running. When a call returns, its frame is popped, so frames do not accumulate. At any moment the stack holds only one chain of calls, from the first down to the current one, and the longest such chain, the depth, sets the space.
  • hanoi(20) makes 221 - 1 calls, but each chain goes 20, 19, …, 0 and returns before the next branch starts, so its stack space is O(n).
  • Depths: factorial(n) n + 1 frames, O(n); fast power(x, n) about log₂ n frames, O(log n); hanoi(n) about n frames, O(n).
  • Raising the limit does not make the real stack underneath bigger, so a deep enough recursion then crashes the interpreter. The fix is a different design: a loop, or a recursion that is only O(log n) deep.

essays.stem: Three versions of power(x, n): (i) x * power(x, n - 1); (ii) half = power(x, n // 2), then half * half (× x if n is odd); (iii) power(x, n // 2) * power(x, n // 2) (× x if n is odd). For each, write the recurrence and its solution, and say what happens for n = 4,096.
essays.answer:
• (i) T(n) = T(n-1) + c → O(n) calls and multiplications, and n + 1 frames deep: power(2, 4096) raises RecursionError.
  • (ii) T(n) = T(n/2) + c → O(log n): for n = 4,096 it makes 14 calls (exponents 4096, 2048, …, 1, 0) and 14 multiplications, 14 frames deep.
  • (iii) T(n) = 2T(n/2) + c → O(n): two calls on half the input undo the halving. For n = 4,096 it makes 16,383 calls. It is only about 14 deep, so it does not crash, but it is no faster than (i).
  • The lesson: count the recursive calls and their size. Calling once and keeping the result in a variable is what makes (ii) logarithmic.

essays.stem: Rewrite gcd as a loop, and explain why that rewrite is easy. Explain why rewriting hanoi without recursion is harder, and what the loop version must keep for itself.
essays.answer:
• Loop version:
  def gcd_loop(a, b):
      while b != 0:
          a, b = b, a % b
      return a
  • It is easy because gcd is tail-shaped: one call, as its very last action, with nothing to do after it. The arguments of the next call can simply replace the current ones.
  • hanoi branches: after the first recursive call it still has to move the largest disk and make the second call. That pending work is what the call stack remembers, so a loop version must push it onto its own stack (Lecture 06's Stack) and pop it later. This is more code, and harder to read.

essays.stem: Explain why binary_strings(0) must return [""], and subsets([]) must return [[]], rather than []. What goes wrong with [], and how many results do binary_strings(n) and subsets of n items return?
essays.answer:
• The base case is the answer for the smallest input, and it must be right. There is exactly one bit string of length 0 (the empty string "") and one subset of the empty set (the empty set), so each answer is a list holding one item: [""] and [[]].
  • With [] there is nothing to build on: the recursive case makes every result by extending a result of the smaller call, so every level returns [] and the final answer is empty, with no error to warn you.
  • binary_strings(n) returns 2n strings and subsets of n items returns 2n lists: each of the n decisions (0 or 1; out or in) doubles the count, and the count for n = 0 is 20 = 1, which is why the base case holds one item.
